column4: The source's full-weight coin evokes an exact balance; here the scales are set for judgment, and not even a mustard-seed weight is omitted or unjustly treated.
The source's calibrated coin meets the explicit image of the balance of judgment: “الوزن يومئذ الحق” makes truthful weighing the standard.
The underweight side of the source's coin image is realized by people whose scales are light and who lose themselves; the verse states the adverse result.
Like the source's measured coin, deeds are literally weighed here; the heavy scales mark success.
This is the reverse outcome to the source's full-weight coin: light scales mean loss and abiding punishment.
The source's coin weighed at full measure parallels the heavy scales that open the surah's final weighing scene.
This ayah gives the favorable consequence of the heavy measure in 101:6, completing the source's image of sound value receiving its due.
Light scales reverse the source's sound, fully calibrated coin and introduce the failing measure.
The preceding ayah's light scales lead here to “هاوية”; this completes the contrast between the source's proper measure and a debased outcome.
The preceding 18:104 says these people thought they were doing well; this ayah says their deeds are null and receive no “وزنا” on Judgment Day.
The source's correctly weighted coin has a sharp opposite in the “مطففين,” who cheat in measures; this ayah names the fraud.
The preceding warning is made concrete: these people take their full measure from others, the opposite of fair calibration.
They short others when measuring or weighing; this is the exact dishonest reversal of the source's full-weight standard.
The source's balanced coin finds a cosmic counterpart in the “ميزان” placed with the raised heaven.
This continues the balance image by forbidding transgression in the scale, the boundary that keeps measure just.
The command to establish weight with justice and not reduce the balance makes the source's exact-weight coin an ethical measure too.
The source describes a coin that is neither short nor excessive; this commands full measure and weighing with the straight balance.
This opens the same practical measuring scene as the source's accurately adjusted coin, requiring full measure.
The next command specifies the source's full-weight image: weigh with the straight balance.
This ayah forbids reducing people's due after the measuring commands, naming the fraud opposite to the source's exact calibration.
The command to give full measure and weight in just balance directly parallels the source's coin assessed at its proper weight.
This continuation forbids diminishing people's due, the commercial fraud opposite to the source's exact calibration.
The people of Midian are told to give full measure and weight and not diminish people's goods; this is the same fair-assessment standard as the coin image.
The command “وأوفوا الكيل والميزان بالقسط” gives a just-measure counterpart to the source's full-weight coin.
The source's weighing image applies even at the smallest scale: a deed of “مثقال ذرة” of good is seen and therefore cannot be lost from the account.
The corresponding particle-weight of evil is also seen; this is the adverse side of the source's account, where nothing escapes assessment.
The source pairs believers' good work with a lasting wage; this ayah likewise joins faith and righteous action to reward, adding “لا يظلمون نقيرا.”
The source glosses أَجْرٌ as the wage for work; this promise says God will not waste the wage of anyone who does good work.
The source quotes this exact promise: those who endure receive their wages “بغير حساب,” a payment not cut down by reckoning.
This repeats the source's combination of faith, good work, and an “أجر غير ممنون,” directly clarifying its unshortened wage.
This ayah also promises “أجر غير ممنون” for believers who do good; it is a close repeated formulation of the source's wage image.
Believers who do good are paid their wages in full here, making explicit the source's claim that righteous work receives its due.
The source's dictionary gloss links work and wage; this gives a concrete case, requiring payment of wages to women who nurse the child.
This independently repeats the wage for nursing work, a direct example of the source's work-for-payment relation.
The source begins with the marketplace and pricing; this ayah calls faithful worship and giving a “تجارة لن تبور,” a trade that does not fail.
The trade in 35:29 is completed by this ayah's promise to pay the traders' wages in full and increase them; the verse contributes the settlement.
The market image becomes an explicit divine transaction: God “اشترى” believers' lives and property for Paradise, so the reader sees faith and effort as a sale with a promised return.
The source's accepted counterfeit is a failed valuation; here those who buy misguidance find “فما ربحت تجارتهم,” a trade with no profit.
The source's coin tests what something is worth; this ayah condemns people who sell God's covenant and oaths for a small price, trading away their share in the Hereafter.
Trade and sale are named directly, then set against fear of the day of account; this joins the source's marketplace and final reckoning.
The people occupied with trade in 24:37 receive this ayah's payoff: God rewards their best deeds and increases them from His bounty.
The source's market vocabulary meets the explicit offer “تجارة تنجيكم”; this ayah frames belief and effort as a salvific transaction.
This specifies what the trade in 61:10 asks for—faith and striving with wealth and selves—linking effort to its return.
The trade described in 61:10–11 is settled here with forgiveness and the promised gardens; this ayah supplies the return on the transaction.
The source's dictionary form عَمَلٌ links work to its wage; this says a person has only what they strive for, the work side of the account.
The preceding striving is to be seen here, so the work is presented for assessment before recompense.
This completes the sequence with full recompense for the striving in 53:39; the source's labor-and-wage image is explicit.
The source links deeds to wages; this says no soul is wronged and people are repaid only for what they did.
Every soul is paid for what it earned, with no injustice and swift accounting; this closely matches the source's final fair settlement.
On return to God every soul is paid in full for what it earned and is not wronged, a concise counterpart to the source's closed account.
At the gathering, each soul is paid in full for what it earned and none is wronged; the verse makes the source's equitable wage concrete.
This day each soul receives the full result of its work without injustice, matching the source's promise of an unshortened settlement.
The source's العمل / أجر connection meets this statement that every soul is paid for what it did; the judge knows their deeds.
Creation is followed by recompense for each soul's earnings without wrong; this joins the source's created human and just final valuation.
Those who endure are paid according to the best of what they did; it specifies the source's work-and-wage link and contrasts passing gain with what is with God.
The promise of good life and wages for believers' best work develops the source's reward for righteous labor.
God does not wrong even an atom's weight, doubles good, and grants a great wage; the smallest measure here safeguards the source's complete payment.
The opened record omits neither small nor large deeds and God wrongs no one; it shows how the source's final account leaves no value unexamined.
A soul faces what it earned and cannot have its ransom accepted; this sets a limit beside the source's image of dues and final settlement.
Wrongdoers would offer all the earth as ransom, but judgment is made justly; this gives the source's payment-and-verdict image its boundary for those who owe an account.
The source glosses د ي ن as debt-dealing in giving or taking; this ayah uses “تداينتم بدين” for a debt due at a term and orders it recorded.
The source's debt gloss includes giving; this calls for a “قرضا حسنا” to God and promises its multiplication, making lending and return concrete.
A goodly loan to God is multiplied and followed by a noble reward, a close Qur'anic instance of the source's debt-and-compensation sense.
This repeats the lending image and promises multiplication and forgiveness, reinforcing the source's sense of payment returned.
The command to offer God a goodly loan is followed by finding good sent ahead and a greater reward, linking lending to later settlement.
The source cites “غير مدينين” as denial of being held to account; this challenge asks the deniers to return the soul if they are not indebted or answerable.
The source identifies “لمدينون” as asking whether they will receive their due; this speaker's incredulous question voices that same resistance to recompense.
The source explains الدِّين as repayment and recompense; “يوم الدين” names the day on which that settlement belongs to God.
The source describes people challenged for denying repayment; these speakers ask mockingly when the “يوم الدين” will be, voicing the same resistance.
The speakers confess that they used to deny the Day of Recompense, a direct example of the denial challenged in the source's account of الدِّين.
This names the Day of Recompense and asks what will make it understood, sharing the source's focus on the reality of the final account.
The next ayah repeats the question about the Day of Recompense; its repetition stresses the day whose settlement the source describes.
This answers the preceding repeated question by describing a day when no soul can help another and command belongs to God, completing the account's finality.
After the warning about cheating measures in 83:1–3, this asks whether the cheaters expect to be raised, tying the dishonest balance to reckoning.
This specifies the resurrection in 83:4 as a great day, giving the weighing fraud a judgment horizon.
The great day is the day people stand before the Lord of the worlds; it completes the link between 83's false measures and the source's final accounting.
In the same surah that condemns short measure, this names those who deny “بيوم الدين,” joining false weighing to the source's repayment day.
This combines return, “الحكم,” and the swiftest accounting; the source likewise closes its image with return before the just judge and final reckoning.
The source cites this return to God; the next ayah supplies the account, so this verse contributes the return that begins the settlement.
This says the account is God's after the return in 88:25, completing the source's pairing of return and reckoning.
The source glosses ح ك م as judgment by justice; this asks “ومن أحسن من الله حكما,” directly echoing the question of the best judge.
God alone has judgment and is the best of decision-makers; this parallels the source's final claim that judgment belongs to the just judge.
David is commanded to judge between people with truth, and warned about forgetting the Day of Account; this brings just judgment and reckoning together.
The people are judged with truth here; the following ayah pays each soul for its deeds, giving the source's just account a parallel scene.
God judges in truth while those invoked besides Him cannot judge; this makes the source's claim of God's uniquely sound judgment concrete.
The source moves from the human in best measure to the lowest state; this creation sequence ends with some returned to the most decrepit age, a bodily reversal.
God creates people, then some are returned to the feeblest age and forget what they knew; this is a direct decline from the source's well-formed human.
Long life can invert a person's creation here; “ننكسه في الخلق” makes a reversal of the source's best-form image explicit.
Human life passes from weakness to strength and back to weakness and gray hair, a specific reversal of the source's high-to-low human trajectory.
The source's “best calibration” for the human has a close counterpart in being created, proportioned, and balanced: “فعدلك.”
This continues the formation in 82:7 by saying God composed the person in whatever form He willed, clarifying the source's image of fitted creation.
God creates and proportionally forms here, a close parallel to the source's human made in “أحسن تقويم.”
Creation is followed by determining and guiding; this makes the measured order behind the source's creation image explicit.
The source's خ ل ق dictionary branch describes a share measured for each; this says God created everything and determined it with precise determination.
This joins the source's creation root to measure directly: “خلقناه بقدر” says everything created is by measure.
The source's image of a human made in best measure parallels “أحسن كل شيء خلقه” and the beginning of human creation here.
He creates and shapes human beings, making their forms beautiful; this gives a direct creation-and-valuation counterpart to the source's best-form image.
This repeated formulation says God shaped people and made their forms beautiful, a direct parallel to the source's valuation of human form.
God's honoring of Adam's children establishes their high worth, a useful boundary against the source's later fall to the lowest state.
Human life and death are made a test of who is best in deed; this explains why the source's fitting and subsequent weighing lead to reward or loss.
The source's dictionary sense of خَلَق as an apportioned share is made concrete by God distributing livelihoods among people in worldly life.
The source describes each person's measured share; here people receive a share of what they earned and God is swift in account.
The source's dictionary form الخلاق means a measured share; this verse says men and women each have a share of what they earn.
The source's share gloss is concretely echoed by the allotted share of inheritance given to men and women.
The inheritance portions here are fixed by stated ratios, a legal instance of the source's measured share assigned to each person.
This continues the inheritance allotments with explicit fractions for spouses and siblings, extending the measured shares in the preceding ayah.
The final inheritance ruling assigns siblings specified portions, another concrete instance of shares measured for each.
The source's dictionary gloss says each person's share is measured; this states that everything has a measure with God.
Provision is sent down only in known measure, a specific parallel to the source's measured allocation of each person's share.
God has set a measure for everything, echoing the source's claim that allotted shares are measured.

The connection is analogical: the source's apparently accepted coin is exposed as false when assessed, while this scene's apparent water proves to be a mirage when reached; both reverse an expected value.
The source's counterfeit becomes valueless when tested; here deeds people thought valuable are made “هباء منثورا,” a specific reversal of their assumed worth.
The source's coin scene names dirhams and tests their worth; Joseph is sold for counted dirhams at a low price, making the undervaluing of a human explicit.
After 101:9 ends with the light-scaled person's destination, this identifies al-Hawiyah as a blazing fire and completes that outcome.
This ayah says the losers thought they were doing well while their effort was lost; 18:105 supplies the source-related verdict that their deeds receive no weight.
The source hears مَمْنُونٍ as an unshortened, measured wage; this promises the Prophet an “أجر غير ممنون,” repeating that wage formulation.
The source's labor-and-wage image has a parallel in spending: what is spent is repaid in full and the giver is not wronged.
This joins patience and righteous work to forgiveness and a great wage, another concrete formulation of the source's labor receiving its due.
The return is measured here: a good deed earns tenfold while evil earns only its like, and no one is wronged.
God recompenses wrongdoers for their deeds and gives good-doers the best reward, a direct two-sided settlement like the source's account.
After describing the believers' costly mobilization, this says God does not waste the wage of the good-doers; 9:121 records even small expenses and journeys.
This specifies what the previous verse's wage covers: every small or large expense and valley crossed is recorded before reward is paid.
The believers rejoice that God does not waste the believers' reward, a specific parallel to payment that is not withheld.
Believers who do good are promised recompense for their best deeds, directly extending the source's work-and-wage relation.
At the gathering people are called with their records and are not wronged even by a thread's weight, joining the source's account with exact measure.
The source frames final settlement through owing and repayment; this says every soul is held in pledge for what it earned.
This repeats the liability image: each person is pledged for what they earned, a specific counterpart to the source's debt-and-account sense.
The source names أَجْرٌ as work's wage; here a worker is assessed as strong and trustworthy before being hired, linking human valuation to paid work.
The employment agreement uses the source's أجر root for serving a stated term; it makes the work-for-return relation concrete.
The fixed one-fifth allocation of the spoils is a concrete instance of the source's dictionary gloss that a share is measured out for each.
This assigns heirs their portion of what parents and relatives leave, a direct instance of the source's measured-share sense.
The division of captured property among specified recipients makes the source's allotted-share image concrete and states that it should not circulate only among the rich.
Provision is sent down in measure for people; this is a specific economic counterpart to the source's claim that shares are allotted by measure.
God expands provision for some and restricts it for others; this makes the source's measured allocation concrete and contrasts it with people judging worldly abundance as ultimate value.
The source uses ق و م for pricing and exact adjustment; this verse uses قواما for balanced spending, a related but different sense of measured proportion.
The source's market tests what a thing is worth; this forbids exchanging God's covenant for a small price and says what is with God is better.
This describes people selling revelation for a small price and losing the promised divine address and purification, a failed bargain that parallels the source's worthless coin.
Those who cast the covenant behind their backs and sell it for a small price enact the source's image of misvaluing what is entrusted to them.
The deeds of disbelievers are compared to ash scattered by wind, leaving them with no power over what they earned; this is a specific image of value dissipating at assessment.
After 83:1–6 links cheating weights with resurrection, this names the record of the wicked, extending the measuring scene into a recorded verdict.
This calls the wicked person's record a written register, specifying how the verdict introduced in 83:7 is kept.
The corresponding record for the righteous is in Illiyyun, giving the source's separate bad valuation a positive counterpart.
This also identifies the righteous record as written, completing the parallel with the wicked register in 83:9.
Hypocrites are assigned the lowest depth of the Fire; this gives “the lowest” in the source's fall image a concrete eschatological counterpart.
People who fail to use their hearts, eyes, and ears are likened to cattle or worse, a specific moral descent from the source's best-formed human.
The same comparison says many people are like cattle or further astray, another direct reversal of the source's elevated human measure.
The source links خ ل ق to measured allotment; this says God creates the human from a drop and determines him, joining human formation to measure.
The stages of human formation culminate in a new creation and the praise “أحسن الخالقين,” a close parallel to the source's excellent human form.
This describes the human's creation from dust and stages of life, then notes that some are returned to decrepit age, joining the source's fit form to its decline.
